sqlc_intro: Super-administrator tool: convert a full-system Excel template into a SQL script, and run SQL scripts directly against the database.
sqlc_caution_body: Statements run with full database privileges. Before any script that changes the database, an automatic restore point (full backup) is created — you can revert to it below at any time. A script counts as read-only only when it is proven read-only: a SELECT that calls a VOLATILE function (one that writes, nextval, setval…) counts as a write and triggers the restore point. Transaction-safe scripts run atomically (any error rolls the whole script back); statements that PostgreSQL forbids in a transaction (VACUUM, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, CREATE DATABASE, ALTER SYSTEM…) run one by one and are automatically reverted from the restore point if one fails. Pasted BEGIN/COMMIT are stripped. Use Dry run to preview: the transaction is rolled back, so no row is saved — with one exception PostgreSQL cannot roll back: sequence values consumed or set (nextval, setval) do not go back. The page names those calls for you. Every run is recorded in the audit log.
sqlc_appendonly_body: system_logs (hash-chained), assessment_history, review_signatures and self_assessment_events are immutable history. The list is not copied by hand: it is resolved from the database (any table carrying the append-only triggers belongs to it). Refused: UPDATE/DELETE/TRUNCATE/ALTER/DROP on those tables; disabling a trigger; changing session_replication_role (which would switch every trigger off at once); and any write aimed at a view built on one of them — the target is recognised by what it actually reaches, not by the name written in the text. Refused in the same way: the body of a function or procedure carrying any of those gestures (it is SQL that will run later, with the same rights); anything aimed at the guard's own objects (schema audit_guard, registry append_only_registry, guard functions); and anything that leaves SQL to reach the server — COPY … TO/FROM PROGRAM, COPY … TO a file, lo_export(). Reverting a restore point does not roll them back either (see Restore points below). No statement this page accepts can erase or rewrite the record of what was done.
sqlc_excel_h2: Generate SQL from an Excel template
sqlc_excel_body: Upload a filled full-system Excel template (the same one used by Import → Full System). Instead of importing it, you get an idempotent SQL script you can review, copy, or run below.
sqlc_file_aria: Excel template file to convert to SQL
sqlc_script_body: Paste or edit SQL below. Multiple statements are allowed (separate with ;).
sqlc_dry_run: Dry run (preview & roll back — no row is saved)
sqlc_rp_body: A full database backup taken automatically before each database-changing script (last 20 kept). Every point carries the name of the database it came from and is filed in that database's own folder; before any restore, that origin is re-read from the file itself and a point taken from another database is refused. A point with no recorded origin shows “—”: it is neither assumed to be ours nor deleted automatically.
sqlc_db_unknown_title: Origin not recorded: this restore point was taken before the origin was stored. It is verified from the file before any restore.
sqlc_warn_volatile: This script calls VOLATILE functions ({{fns}}): it is treated as a write (a restore point is taken). On a dry run, the rollback does not give back sequence values that were consumed.
sqlc_prerevert: Current state backed up before the revert as
sqlc_rp_undo_body: The operational database goes back to the restore point: employees, roles, skills, assessments, plans, settings and every other table. Anything created or changed since that point is lost — but the current state is itself backed up just before, into a point named pre-revert-…, which is shown to you.
sqlc_rp_keep_body: The append-only audit trail — system_logs, assessment_history, review_signatures, self_assessment_events, and any other table carrying the append-only triggers — is copied out before the restore and re-attached to the database afterwards, with its hash chain intact. History is not rewound: the record that the change happened, and that you reverted it, both survive. If a preserved row can no longer be re-attached because the revert deleted the employee, skill or review it describes, the revert says so and keeps those rows in a quarantine schema — they are never silently dropped.
sqlc_generated_ok: SQL generated and loaded into the editor below. Review it, then Run.
sqlc_write_confirm: This will WRITE to a test instance (not a dry run). Continue?
sqlc_banner_dry: Dry run — all changes were rolled back; nothing was saved.
sqlc_auto_reverted: The database was automatically reverted to the restore point taken before the run — no partial changes remain. The append-only audit trail was preserved across the revert, so this failed run stays on the record.
sqlc_restore_point_created: Restore point created before this run:
sqlc_restore_point_created_tail: — revert from the list below if needed.
sqlc_rp_empty: No restore points yet — one is created automatically before your first database-changing script.
sqlc_revert_warning:
Revert the database to restore point “%s”?

WILL be undone: every operational table — employees, roles, skills, assessments, plans, settings. Anything created or changed since that point is LOST and cannot be recovered.

Will NOT be undone: the append-only audit trail (system_logs, assessment_history, review_signatures, self_assessment_events). It is preserved across the restore and re-attached afterwards, so the record of the change — and of this revert — survives.
sqlc_preserve_partial: audit row(s) re-attached, but {{n}} could NOT be ({{detail}}) — the employees, skills or reviews they describe no longer exist after the revert. They were not deleted: they are kept in schema {{schema}}, and this is recorded in the audit log. The next revert is blocked until that schema is reconciled.
sqlc_preserve_ok: Append-only audit trail preserved: {{n}} row(s) re-attached after the restore, none lost.
sqlc_column_privilege: Refused: this table has secret columns (password hashes, tokens…). Replace “*” with the list of columns you need.
sqlc_secret_refused: Refused: this query reads or changes secret data (sessions, second factors, tokens, password hashes, API keys, SSO secrets, HRIS credentials or secret settings). The SQL console never gives access to them; they are managed from their own pages. The refusal is recorded in the audit log.
